summary: Defines a convention for carrying SNMP packets over the transport provided by Novell's IPX protocol. This lets management stations talk to agents on IPX networks. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 1420.

plainLanguage.summary: SNMP messages normally travel in one kind of envelope. This document shows how to put them in the envelope used by Novell networks so they can be delivered there too.

subtitle: Carrying SNMP messages on Novell IPX networks.

tldr.problem: SNMP normally runs over UDP/IP, but many networks in the 1990s used Novell NetWare, which runs on IPX, a connectionless transport similar to UDP.
tldr.mechanism: Define socket numbers in IPX for SNMP: port 36879 (hex 900F) for query messages, port 36880 (hex 9010) for traps. SNMP messages are carried unchanged in IPX datagrams.
tldr.outcome: Management stations could monitor agents on IPX networks without adding a full IP stack. The document is informational and was replaced by RFC 1420.

today: RFC 1298 is informational and was replaced by RFC 1420. As IPX networks were phased out in favor of IP, this specification became obsolete.

sections.title: The Problem
sections.content:
In the early 1990s, Novell NetWare was widely deployed in local area networks, yet it did not support the Internet Protocol. IPX (Internetwork Packet Exchange), Novell's connectionless datagram protocol, was roughly equivalent to UDP in function. Organizations running NetWare networks needed a way to manage devices on those networks using SNMP, the standard network management protocol.

This RFC specifies how to carry SNMP messages directly over IPX, allowing management stations to monitor SNMP agents on IPX networks. The specification assigns IPX socket addresses for SNMP operations, similar to how UDP port numbers are used in the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: Novell networks didn't have UDP, but they had IPX, which does the same job. This shows how to send SNMP management commands through IPX.

sections.title: Socket Assignments and Packet Types
sections.content:
SNMP agents listen on IPX socket 36879 (hexadecimal 900F) for GetRequest-PDU, GetNextRequest-PDU, and SetRequest-PDU messages. They listen on socket 36880 (hexadecimal 9010) for Trap-PDU messages sent by other agents.

GetResponse-PDU messages are addressed back to the socket and IPX address from which the original request came. All SNMP packets set the IPX packet type field to 4 (Packet Exchange Packet), indicating a standard IPX datagram. The SNMP message itself is encoded identically to UDP-based SNMP; only the transport layer changes.
sections.plainLanguage: SNMP uses mailboxes called sockets: 36879 for commands, 36880 for alerts. The replies go back to whoever sent the command.

sections.title: Message Size and Compatibility
sections.content:
IPX supports a maximum datagram length of 546 bytes, which imposes a limit on SNMP message size. Although the SNMP specification itself allows messages to be as short as 484 bytes, this RFC recommends that implementations support the full 546-byte IPX limit. This maximum is also the packet size guaranteed to traverse IPX routers without fragmentation.

The agent-addr field in Trap-PDU messages emitted by SNMP agents running over IPX should contain 0.0.0.0. The management station can determine the source of the trap by querying the IPX transport layer directly. This is necessary because IPX addresses differ from IP addresses and there is no standard way to embed an IPX address in the agent-addr field.
sections.plainLanguage: IPX messages can be at most 546 bytes, so SNMP messages are limited to that size. When an agent sends an alert, it can't put its IPX address in the standard place, so the manager has to ask IPX where it came from.
